reader.title: Lynching of John Watson
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
bases: Railroad laborers captured John Watson, tried him before an improvised court and hanged him (A1, A5, A9); no paper states the race of anyone involved, so the case's place in a study of anti-Black violence is doubtful.

Watson was hanged by railroad men after a trial by an improvised court with a jury of railroad men, with over 200 attending (A1, A5); the Crawford Avalanche says he was 'hanged by a mob' (A11). The accusation of robbery and attempted murder served as the pretext of justice.

The local Hailey Wood River Times account (A1) and the independent Dakota wire (A5, A6, A9) agree on the robbery of Fox, the pursuit, the improvised trial and Watson's hanging, though they differ on place and date.

summary.text: The lynching of John Watson took place about October 27, 1882, when railroad laborers on the Oregon Short Line hanged him at the Kelton road crossing, about ten miles below Patton's station, after an improvised trial.
Watson was accused of shooting and robbing a fellow laborer, William Fox, and his alleged accomplice, Cash Austin, was handed to a deputy sheriff and later freed.
A wire story three weeks later carried the case to eastern papers, placing it at "Pattersons Station" with a Yankton, Dakota dateline.

Watson and Austin were grading hands who, according to the Wood River Times of Hailey, worked on the grade only when they were broke and followed the railroad camps from Granger as "sagebrush gamblers."
Watson had been Fox's "partner" for months, sleeping and eating with him.
No article states the race of Watson, Austin, Fox or the men who hanged Watson.

At dusk on a Thursday, as Fox walked back from the Kelton road crossing, where he had bought clothes, he was shot in the wrist and side and robbed of over $200; the local paper charged Watson with firing the shots.
Fox reached Hale, Smith & Co.'s camp and told his story, and a posse of railroad hands captured both men after an all-night chase, after which Fox identified them.
Austin was said to have refused at first to help until Watson threatened to kill him.
The laborers improvised a court, and a jury of railroad men condemned Watson to be hanged near the scene and ordered Austin turned over to the authorities.
Watson was then led with a noose around his neck from the camp to the Kelton crossing and hanged about 3 p.m. on Friday, in sight of the place of the robbery, with over 200 men attending.
A couple of hours later his body was stripped of its clothes and left hanging.
Austin was taken to Hailey in the charge of a deputy sheriff, and the Ketchum Keystone reported on November 17 that he had been liberated, being said to have been forced into the crime by Watson.
No report of an inquest or of any action against the men who hanged Watson appears in the coverage.
The Wood River Times ran the story under "LYNCHING ON THE O. S. L." and called the hanging an "execution."

It quoted a correspondent at Elizabeth post office who wrote that "a regiment of soldiers could not have saved him" and that the people were determined to stop the shooting and robbing along the line.
The Ketchum Keystone reprinted the account on November 3 under "Lynching on the Oregon Short Line."
In mid-November a wire dated at Yankton, Dakota, reached eastern papers, with the Daily Gazette heading it "LYNCH COURT." and the Washington Evening Critic giving "two hundred spectators."

The Somerset Herald's version placed the lynching at "Pattersons Station, I. T." and said Watson was "hanged to a telegraph pole," while a Michigan paper reduced it to one line in a crime column, saying he was "hanged by a mob at Patterson, Dakota."
None of these reports used racial terms or commented on the hanging.

The accounts differ on place and date: the local Hailey paper of October 30 placed the hanging near Patton's station in Idaho on the preceding Friday, while the Dakota wire of November 19 called it "yesterday" and gave "Pattersons Station" or "Patterson, Dakota."
Because the local report appeared three weeks before the wire and names the camp, crossing and county seat involved, it is the stronger evidence for both.

accounts.label: Local account (Wood River Times, Hailey)
accounts.gist: Robbery near Billingsley's on Thursday evening; posse captured both after an all-night chase; a jury of railroad men condemned Watson, who was hanged at the Kelton crossing about 3 p.m. Friday before over 200 men.

accounts.label: Wire report (Yankton, Dakota)
accounts.gist: Laborers captured the robbers, tried them before an impromptu court, and hanged Watson to a telegraph pole at 'Pattersons Station'; Austin was turned over to the authorities.

framing.detail: The Wood River Times reported the hanging as an 'execution' after a trial and quoted a correspondent that 'a regiment of soldiers could not have saved him' and that the people meant to stop robbery along the line.
Eastern papers ran the Dakota wire under 'LYNCH COURT.' or 'Hanged.' in brief, without comment.

info: Robbery on a Thursday evening and hanging about 3 p.m. the next day, Friday; the Wood River Times of Monday, Oct. 30, 1882 calls it 'last Thursday', which points to Oct. 26-27, 1882. The wire dated Nov. 18-19 says 'yesterday'.

Kelton road crossing, about 10 miles below Patton's station, near Billingsley's (Elizabeth post office) and Hale, Smith & Co.'s grading camp on the Oregon Short Line (local account); 'Pattersons Station, I. T.' or 'Patterson, Dakota' (wire).
John Watson, a railroad grading hand and 'sagebrush gambler'; race not stated.
Accused with Cash Austin of shooting, wounding and robbing fellow laborer William Fox of over $200.
Railroad laborers: a posse raised at Hale, Smith & Co.'s camp, an improvised court and a jury of railroad men.
Cash Austin was turned over to the authorities and later liberated, said to have been forced by Watson to take part.

sources.note: Fullest and earliest local account: robbery of Fox near Billingsley's, posse, improvised court, Watson hanged at the Kelton crossing before over 200 men; Austin sent to Hailey.
quotes: The jury of railroad men condemned Watson to be hung near the scene of the robbery and attempted murder, and ordered that Austin be turned over to the authorities for trial.
Feeling ran very high, and a regiment of soldiers could not have saved him.
